analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil drilling along most U.S. coasts and requires cars to average 55 mpg by 2030.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: with no cosponsors, it died in the Senate Energy Committee after its May 2010 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: Written just weeks after the Deepwater Horizon oil disaster, the bill would have permanently barred new oil and gas leasing off the Pacific and Atlantic coasts and in parts of the Gulf of Mexico. It also would have required new cars and trucks to reach a fleet average of 55 miles per gallon by 2030, and directed regulators to set the strictest fuel and emissions standards technology could achieve. The bill's own findings argued that drilling would save consumers only pennies at the pump while efficiency standards would save dollars.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities whose beaches, fishing grounds, and tourism economies are exposed to spill risk, and drivers who would save money on gasoline as vehicles became more efficient. The bill cited government figures that a 55 mpg standard would save consumers the equivalent of $1.43 or more per gallon by 2030, versus about 3 cents per gallon from expanded offshore drilling.

how_it_helps.text: Permanently prohibits new oil and gas leases and permits in the Pacific and Atlantic outer Continental Shelf regions and protected Gulf of Mexico areas, removing future spill risk from those waters [S2][S3].
Requires automakers to reach a combined fleet average of at least 55 miles per gallon by model year 2030, replacing standards that were set to phase in more slowly [S2][S3].

Directs EPA and the Transportation Department to set the strongest vehicle emission and fuel-efficiency standards achievable with available technology for model year 2017 onward, weighing costs [S2][S3].

The bill's findings, citing the Energy Information Administration, estimate the 55 mpg standard would save consumers the equivalent of $1.43 or more per gallon by 2030, while opening all the restricted coastal areas to drilling would save only about 3 cents per gallon [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies lose access to new federal offshore leases along the Atlantic, Pacific, and much of the Gulf, and automakers face much steeper engineering costs to meet a 55 mpg fleet average by 2030. Some of that cost could be passed to new-car buyers, and critics of high fuel-economy mandates often argue buyers who want larger vehicles face fewer choices and higher prices.

drawbacks.text: A 55 mpg fleet average by 2030 was far above the standards then in place, and automakers would bear significant engineering and production costs, some of which would likely show up in new-vehicle prices [S2][S3].

Banning drilling outright forfeits domestic oil production — the bill itself estimates the restricted areas could yield about 500,000 barrels per day by 2030 — which would keep some U.S. supply dependent on imports [S3].
The bill's consumer savings figures come from its own legislative findings, which are advocacy documents prepared by the sponsor rather than an independent analysis [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded real but gradual consumer savings at the gas pump and protection of coastal waters against higher new-car prices and forgone domestic oil production. Its core argument — that efficiency standards save drivers far more per gallon than coastal drilling would — is laid out in its own findings, though those figures are the sponsor's case, not an neutral estimate. The design was straightforward; the main question was whether the mandated pace was feasible for automakers, which the bill addressed by allowing regulators to weigh costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on May 27, 2010, about five weeks after the Deepwater Horizon rig disaster began spilling oil into the Gulf of Mexico [S1][S5][S3].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor — the bill lists zero cosponsors for its entire life [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced; that was the last action of any kind [S5].
The bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies kept the legal path open to future Atlantic, Pacific, and Gulf leasing proposals, and automakers faced no new 55 mpg mandate. The Obama administration did move toward tougher fuel-economy rules through regulation later, but this bill itself changed nothing.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill during the Gulf oil spill to ban coastal leasing and raise fuel-economy standards; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill to expire at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Bernie Sanders
against.what_they_did: Did not secure a single cosponsor, leaving the bill with no visible coalition to push the committee to act.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a vote, so no party split was ever recorded; its lack of cosponsors from either party suggests no broad base of support in either caucus.

industries.note: The bill permanently closes Atlantic, Pacific, and much of the Gulf outer Continental Shelf to new leasing, cutting off future drilling territory. Oil producers kept that territory open because the bill died.

A 55 mpg fleet average by 2030 would have forced major engineering spending, but it also would have set a single national standard with long lead time. Automakers bore no new mandate because the bill never moved.

Removing new offshore leases along the coasts reduces the risk of spills that would damage beaches, fisheries, and tourism economies — a risk made vivid by the Deepwater Horizon disaster the bill responded to. They lost that protection when the bill died.
